name: Ibibio
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 7 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Harris, John, Eno-Abasi Urua & Kevin Tang. 2023. A unified model of lenition as modulation reduction: gauging consonant strength in Ibibio. Phonology 40(1-2): 35-64. doi:10.1017/S095267572400006X (Cambridge Core PDF; identical text in the 2022 OSF preprint doi:10.31234/osf.io/a25yw)
catalog_locator: p. 43, sec. 4 'Lenition in Ibibio'; p. 46, sec. 4; p. 58, sec. 6 'Conclusion'
catalog_quote: In Ibibio, the basic template takes the form C1V1XC2V2, where X is a copy of either V1 (CVVCV) or C2 (CVCCV). The resemblance to a heavy-light trochee is unmistakable, as has been pointed out by Urua (1990, 2000) and Akinlabi & Urua (1992, 1994). Similar observations have been made about the closely related language Efik (Cook 1985; Hyman 1990). As a lexical-tone language, Ibibio lacks stress prominence, the property most usually associated with the metrical foot. Nevertheless, the CVXCV template does display weight and segmental asymmetries that are strongly reminiscent of trochees in stress languages. For example, the second syllable of the template must be light, while the first can and, in certain paradigms, must be heavy. A full range of vowel contrasts is supported in the first syllable but not in the second. Lenition, as we will see presently, occurs in stem positions that correspond to weak positions in metrical trochees. It is debatable whether these facts indicate that Ibibio actually has metrical feet. The stem template might instead reflect a universally preferred prosodic shape for root+suffix combinations (Downing 2006). ... A tone language such as Ibibio illustrates how segmental asymmetries can signal accentual prominence even in the absence of stress (cf. Hyman 2008; Downing 2010; Harris & Hyman 2022).
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Ibibio (ibib1240) is not in the catalog. The six title-keyword items reduce to four works: (a) Akinlabi & Urua 2003 'Foot structure in the Ibibio verb' (three duplicate Glottolog records), paywalled at de Gruyter (Unpaywall is_oa=False; no author copy found; (b) Gibbon 2022 'New Perspectives on Ibibio Speech Rhythm' (Springer Festschrift, author's copy downloaded from Gibbon's Bielefeld page) — rhythm-formant/PVI study, silent on word-stress placement; (c) Gut, Urua, Adouakou & Gibbon 2002 'Rhythm in West African tone languages' (TAPS proceedings, downloaded from the same page) — syllable-timing metrics, silent on word stress; (d) Akinlabi 1995 'Prosodic truncation and template satisfaction' — print-only Festschrift chapter, medium priority. Both downloaded PDFs, their text extractions and a one-page Rosetta orthography excerpt are and. The best first-hand stress statement read in this search of works with stress in the title remains Harris, Urua & Tang 2023 (Phonology 40, p.43, already held by the project): 'As a lexical-tone language, Ibibio lacks stress prominence' — i.e. no word stress; tone language with a heavy-light CVXCV stem template.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Ibibio is a lexical-tone language (two level tones H/L plus downstep) with no stress prominence; the only foot-like organisation is the verb stem's CVXCV heavy-light (trochee-like) template, diagnosed by syllable weight, vowel-contrast licensing and consonant lenition in the second (weak) syllable, not by stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None; no stress of any degree is posited.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. The authors note it is 'debatable' whether the trochee-like stem template constitutes genuine metrical feet (it may reflect a universal preferred root+suffix shape, Downing 2006).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is about the language's word prosody generally (lexical tone, no stress); the trochee-like template is a property of the inflectional verb stem (root + optional suffix). Urua 2004 JIPA independently describes Ibibio as 'a register terraced level tone language with two level tones' and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Harris, Urua & Tang 2023 and Urua 2004 describe Ibibio proper (ibib1240; Urua's data are the Uruan/Uyo variety of Akwa Ibom State). Not Efik (efik1245) or Anaang (anaa1238), which are separate Lower Cross glottocodes; Urua 2004 notes dialectal variation among Ibibio clans (Ibiono, Uruan, Uyo, Iman, Ikono) mainly in vowels and tone.

tone_statements.citation: Sylvanus, Esther Ubong & Wale Ogunlaye. 2025. Tone systems of Igbo, Yoruba and Ibibio: a comparative analysis and the linguistic implications. Journal of Philosophy, Policy and Strategic Studies (JPPSS), University of Uyo (posted 7 July 2025; volume/issue not shown on the landing page). ISSN 1595-9457 (online), 3043-4211 (print).
tone_statements.quote: This paper aims at providing a comparative analysis of the tonal systems of Igbo, Ibibio, and Yoruba, highlighting their similarities and differences. By examining tone types, distribution and lexical functional load, the analysis aims to contribute to a deeper understanding of tone as a linguistic phenomenon and its implication in language learning. Using a structured corpus, data was obtained by means of elicitation from six consultants (that is, two native speakers of each of the languages, purposively selected).
tone_statements.locator: abstract on the JPPSS landing page

tone_statements.citation: Ekpenyong, Moses, Eno-Abasi Urua, Oliver Watts, Simon King & Junichi Yamagishi. 2014. Statistical parametric speech synthesis for Ibibio. Speech Communication 56: 243-251. doi:10.1016/j.specom.2013.02.003
tone_statements.quote: Tone information. Ibibio is tonal and has high (H), low (L), downstepped high (DH), high-low contour (HL) and low-high contour (LH) tones. In the current implementation of our system, tones are annotated manually for both the training corpus and the test utterances. Native speakers of Ibibio performed the annotation on an utterance-by-utterance basis using the audio recordings for reference.
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2.2 Pronunciation dictionary, 'Tone information' paragraph, p.8 of the author manuscript
tone_statements.summary: TTS paper; lists five tones H, L, downstepped H, HL, LH (contours labelled, not analysed); tense marked by LH/HL on morphemes; no orthographic tone marking; no TBU; stress only re dictionary.

tone_statements.citation: Coombs, Afton L. 2013. High tone processes in Ibibio. Proceedings of Meetings on Acoustics (ICA 2013 Montreal), paper 060232. Acoustical Society of America. doi:10.1121/1.4800734. [written version of the talk abstracted as: Coombs, Afton L. 2013. Downstep exceptions in Ibibio. Journal of the Acoustical Society of America 133(5, Supplement): 3573. doi:10.1121/1.4806555]
tone_statements.quote: Ibibio, a Niger-Congo language spoken in southeastern Nigeria, is a terraced tone language with contrastive H and L tones. H tones in Ibibio experience automatic and non-automatic downstep, lowering both in sequences of high tones and around intervening lows. This study aims to determine those factors which counteract or overrule the downstep process. ... The main finding of this study is that while single words show acoustically measurable downtrends, they also show non-lowering and even raising of high tones, specifically in HHL contexts.
tone_statements.locator: abstract of JASA 133(5 Suppl.): 3573 (doi:10.1121/1.4806555) as delivered in the Crossref record; POMA paper body not

tone_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce. 2002. Tone languages and the universality of intrinsic F0: evidence from Africa. Journal of Phonetics 30(1): 101-129. doi:10.1006/jpho.2001.0156
tone_statements.quote: They are all &&register'' tone languages (Pike, 1948), that is, characterized by systems of level tones. ... Ibibio has two tones, High and Low, with Downstep (here written ) a!ecting H tones. With respect to lexical tone, dialect di!erences consist primarily in that H}L sequences in some dialects correspond to H}HL sequences (i.e., High}Falling) in other dialects, H} H sequences in some dialects and H}H}L in others.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Two level tones (High, Low) plus downstep affecting H; some dialects have H-HL (falling) for others' H-L; F0 measured by tone; nothing on stress. ff prints as '!'.

tone_statements.citation: Urua, Eno-Abasi E. 2002. The tone system of Ibibio. In U. Gut & D. Gibbon (eds.), Typology of African Prosodic Systems (TAPS 2001 Bielefeld Proceedings), 65-85. Bielefeld: Universitat Bielefeld.
tone_statements.quote: In this study, we distinguish between the phonemic tones and the surface phonetic ones. We also maintain that the phonemic tones are High, Low and downstepped High tone while the surface phonetic tones are High, Low, downstepped High, in addition to the contour tones, Low-High and High-Low. Although the downstepped High tone has a restricted distribution, occurring only after a preceding High tone and never in the initial position, we argue that it is contrastive because it contrasts with Low and High tones in the stem as we show in (3).
tone_statements.locator: sec. 2 'Ibibio tone system' right column (second page of the chapter, pp. 65-85; no page numbers printed in this copy)
tone_statements.summary: Terrace-level system: phonemic H, L and contrastive !H; HL/LH contours derived from level tones; downdrift of H and L; floating L behind !H and grammatical floating tones; F0 study. Nothing on stress.

tone_statements.citation: Ekere, Michael Edoabasi (1996/7). Tone patterns in Ibibio noun phrase structures. Journal of West African Languages 26. pp. 45-54.
tone_statements.quote: This study is based on the fact that Ibibio is a register tone language and that tone carries both the lexical and the grammatical load in Ibibio phonology (cf. Pike 1948:5–7, Clark and Yallop 1990:290). ... Ibibio has the level tones low (L), high (H), and downstep (!H) together with rising (LH) and falling (HL) tones. Both simple (L, H) and complex (LH, HL) tones are found in citation forms as well as in units larger than the word. In phrases and in connected speech, there are the phenomena of tone-spread and downdrift which will not be treated in this article.
tone_statements.summary: Author calls Ibibio a register tone language: H, L, downstepped H plus rising LH / falling HL treated as complex (level sequences); floating tones posited; nothing on stress. At least 100 forms.

tone_statements.citation: Urua, Eno E. (1996/7). A phonetic analysis of Ibibio tones: a preliminay investigation. Journal of West African Languages 26. pp. 15-26.
tone_statements.quote: Three contrastive tones arise in phonological analysis in Ibibio H, L, and !H (Urua 1994). The !H tone, however, has a restricted distribution and may only occur after a preceding H tone. Other tonal realisations include a high-low (HL) falling and a low-high (LH) rising contour tones. Each syllable is tone bearing with either a level tone or one of the contour tones. With this, a disyllabic word in Ibibio may have any one of the following patterns, H-H, H-L, H-!H, L-L, and L-H (barring word class restrictions) as in (1a).
tone_statements.summary: Terraced-level system: H, L and downstepped H contrastive (F0 study, 2 speakers); HL/LH contours treated as further realisations/sandhi; automatic downdrift also measured; nothing on stress. At least 75 forms.

tone_statements.citation: Urua, Eno-Abasi E. (1996/97). A phonetic analysis of Ibibio tones: a preliminary investigation. Journal of West African languages 26. pp. 15-26.
tone_statements.quote: Three contrastive tones arise in phonological analysis in Ibibio H, L, and !H (Urua 1994). The !H tone, however, has a restricted distribution and may only occur after a preceding H tone. Other tonal realisations include a high-low (HL) falling and a low-high (LH) rising contour tones. In Moses Effiong Ekpenyong & Imelda Icheji Udoh (eds.), Current Issues in Descriptive Linguistics and Digital Humanities: A Festschrift in Honor of Professor Eno-Abasi Essien Urua, 457-486. Singapore: Springer. (Glottolog id 693490)
sources.quote: Ibibio therefore occupies an intermediate position between languages with affixal morphology (and only traces of prosodic morphology, for instance in the stress system of English and German), on the one hand, and languages with no affixal morphology but contrastive lexical tone like Chinese, on the other hand. [p.464] ... Typologically, the LF spectrum shape in Ibibio resembles that of English and German and contrasts sharply with that of Mandarin Chinese (Gibbon, 2021), indicating the presence of prosodic feet or stress groups in addition to syllable tone [p.468]
sources.locator: pp. 464 and 468 (author's copy of the published chapter; page numbers printed)
sources.note: A speech-rhythm study (Rhythm Formant Analysis of AM/FM envelopes, nPVI/rPVI, hierarchical clustering) of Ibibio counting and read data, not a description of word-stress placement. It places Ibibio typologically 'intermediate' between affixal stress-accent languages (English, German) and non-affixal tone languages (Chinese), and reads the low-frequency spectrum as evidence of 'prosodic feet or stress groups in addition to syllable tone' (p.468); it never states that any syllable of an Ibibio word bears stress, and treats stress-pitch accents as an English property contrasted with Ibibio tone…

sources.citation: Gut, Ulrike, Eno-Abasi Urua, Sandrine Adouakou & Dafydd Gibbon. 2002. Rhythm in West African tone languages: a study of Ibibio, Anyi and Ega. In Ulrike Gut & Dafydd Gibbon (eds.), Typology of African Prosodic Systems (Bielefeld Occasional Papers in Typology 1), 159-165. (Glottolog id 47904, which lists Gibbon as first author; the PDF byline is Gut, Urua, Adouakou & Gibbon)
sources.quote: Vowels undergo assimilation, lengthening, shortening and deletion but not reduction in the sense in which English vowels undergo reduction in unstressed syllables. The tone system fits into a terrace level pattern since it has two level pitches, High and Low plus a contrastive downstepped High tone in addition to two contour tones, High-Low and Low-High.
sources.note: Measures speech rhythm (Rhythm Ratio, Rhythm Index, %V / deltaC) for one speaker each of Anyi, Ega and Ibibio and finds all three strongly syllable-timed (Ibibio RR 66.3, RI 42.4; Table 1, p.163). The Ibibio sketch (sec. 3.3, pp.161-162) gives syllable structure, consonants, vowel length contrast and the two-tone terraced system with downstep; the only stress-related remark is that Ibibio vowels do not reduce as English vowels do in unstressed syllables. No statement of word-stress placement.

tone.quote: This study is based on the fact that Ibibio is a register tone language and that tone carries both the lexical and the grammatical load in Ibibio phonology (cf. Pike 1948:5–7, Clark and Yallop 1990:290). ... Ibibio has the level tones low (L), high (H), and downstep (!H) together with rising (LH) and falling (HL) tones. Both simple (L, H) and complex (LH, HL) tones are found in citation forms as well as in units larger than the word. In phrases and in connected speech, there are the phenomena of tone-spread and downdrift which will not be treated in this article.

tone.quote: Three contrastive tones arise in phonological analysis in Ibibio H, L, and !H (Urua 1994). The !H tone, however, has a restricted distribution and may only occur after a preceding H tone. Other tonal realisations include a high-low (HL) falling and a low-high (LH) rising contour tones. Each syllable is tone bearing with either a level tone or one of the contour tones. With this, a disyllabic word in Ibibio may have any one of the following patterns, H-H, H-L, H-!H, L-L, and L-H (barring word class restrictions) as in (1a).
